rv.q: It offers plenty of laughs, and shows that Lipman has lost none of her stage charisma.

There’s wit and compassion to the piece, which celebrates the uniqueness of this generous, eccentric person and touches on some probing questions about society’s response to those who are different in any way.
And that’s about it, in a production by Stephen Mear that’s heavy on the whimsy and light on everything else.
She also deserves to be in a better play.
Yet, theatrically, it’s still pedestrian fare of a clumping kind.
This remains a joyous and memorable evening of theatre.
Her joyous performance captivates from the opening moments and never loosens its grip.

In all, ALLEGRA proves a pleasant and frequently amusing piece of froth and besides, it’s always a joy to see 80 year old national treasures on stage reminding us how they’ve built their considerable reputations.
Lipman is a delight to watch in this nostalgic and touching play.
But even this redoubtable talent can’t make a satisfying whole of Allegra, Peter Quilter’s bizarre play that dresses up a societal broadside within the broadest possible whimsy.
I found myself grinning from ear to ear from start to finish in what is the perfect tonic for this gloomy world and one of the most joyous shows I have ever seen.
Ultimately, though, it is a sweet show that demands very little from anyone.
But in between these gaudy joyful tent-poles the structure sags dreadfully.

cn.t: Lipman shines in Quilter's lightweight comedy about a singing eccentric, but critics find the play itself sluggish and sitcom-like. Reviews are mixed, praising the star's performance while faulting the uneven script.
